content: Magnesium nitride, with the chemical formula Mg₃N₂, is an inorganic compound composed of magnesium and nitrogen. At standard room temperature and pressure, it appears as a greenish-yellow powder. When exposed to water, magnesium nitride reacts to produce ammonia gas, a characteristic shared by many metal nitrides. The reaction can be represented as follows: Mg₃N₂ + 6H₂O → 3Mg(OH)₂ + 2NH₃. Magnesium nitride can be synthesized by burning magnesium metal in a pure nitrogen atmosphere. The chemical reaction for this process is: 3Mg + N₂ → Mg₃N₂. Additionally, when magnesium is burned in air, a small amount of magnesium nitride is formed alongside the primary product, magnesium oxide. Magnesium nitride played a pivotal role as a catalyst in the first successful synthesis of borazon, also known as cubic boron nitride. Robert H. Wentorf, Jr., while attempting to convert hexagonal boron nitride into its cubic form, employed a combination of heat, pressure, and various catalysts. Despite trying all logical catalysts, including those known to facilitate diamond synthesis, he was unsuccessful. Driven by curiosity and desperation, he adopted what he referred to as the make the maximum number of mistakes approach. He added magnesium wire to hexagonal boron nitride and subjected the mixture to the same heat and pressure treatment. Upon examining the magnesium wire under a microscope, he discovered tiny dark lumps adhering to it. These lumps exhibited the ability to scratch a polished block of boron carbide, a property previously attributed only to diamond. The presence of an ammonia odor, resulting from the reaction of magnesium nitride with moisture in the air, led him to deduce that the magnesium metal had reacted with boron nitride to form magnesium nitride. This compound, in turn, acted as the true catalyst in the synthesis of cubic boron nitride.
